open-question.question: At each of the five multi-call open-question tool sites (review-milestone-requirements, the two annotating passes, the answer sweep, answer-procedure.md), where does the rule "write the full fixed command on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function" sit: once per file in the existing tool-contract sentence, repeated at every fenced call, or somewhere else in the file?

The Claude host renders the {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder as the host-provided reference ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, so the fixed open-question tool command as shipped there already contains one variable. How should the "never through a variable" rule be worded so that it bans variables the runner introduces itself without contradicting the command it sits beside, given that core/ files may name no host?

The answer sweep's per-question lift call lives in core/shared/answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md, which the goal does not list among the multi-call tool sites although the sweep runs it once per question. Does that procedure get the full-command rule too, or is the rule stated only in the five files the goal names?

The complete-task agent (core/agents/complete-task.md) stages its own multi-path change set with git add outside the commit procedure, saying only "naming each path explicitly". Does the literal-path rule extend to that staging site, or does it stay confined to core/shared/commit-procedure.md as the goal words it?

commit-procedure.md shows its two path-taking commands with the whole path set as one token, git status --porcelain -- <PATHS> and git add <PATHS>. Do those example commands keep the single <PATHS> token with the literal-path rule added in prose beside them, or are the examples themselves rewritten to show several separately named paths?
open-question.alternative: Both example commands stay exactly as written, `git status --porcelain -- <PATHS>` in step 1 and `git add <PATHS>` in step 2. The literal-path rule goes in prose next to each command: every path is written out on the command line as its own argument, and none is held in a shell variable. Step 1 also gets the "naming each path explicitly" wording that step 2 already has. It is the smallest edit. The commands keep the same uppercase name, PATHS, that the procedure's Inputs section and all 17 callers' PATHS bullets use, so no caller-facing wording changes. The rule is stated in the step a runner is reading when it builds the command. The command still shows the whole path set as one substitutable token. That is the shape that invites a runner to put the set into one variable and expand it unquoted, so the fix relies on prose overriding what the example shows, at the exact spot where the failure starts.

Both example commands are rewritten to show several separately named placeholders instead of one set token, for example `git status --porcelain -- <PATH_1> <PATH_2> …` and `git add <PATH_1> <PATH_2> …`. They are tied to the Inputs entry as the members of PATHS. The literal-path rule is also stated in prose beside them. The example itself shows one argument per path, so the command shape and the prose rule say the same thing. It stays generic and suggests no particular file set, which fits callers that pass one to four paths, including a whole milestone directory. It adds a numbered-placeholder convention that no other runtime file uses, and its link to the PATHS input has to be explained. The ellipsis and the fixed count of two shown can also be misread as an exact number of arguments.

Both example commands are rewritten to show a realistic set of literal paths in place of any set token. The natural instance is the most common caller pair: `git status --porcelain -- <MILESTONE_DIR>/open_questions.xml <MILESTONE_DIR>/requirements.md` and `git add <MILESTONE_DIR>/open_questions.xml <MILESTONE_DIR>/requirements.md`. Each is marked as an example, and the literal-path rule is stated in prose beside them. It shows exactly what a correct command looks like when it runs, using paths a runner will recognise from its own caller. This leaves the least room for an interpretation that substitutes a variable. The procedure is shared by 17 skills with different path sets: some pass only `milestones/README.md`, a milestone directory, or the principle store. A concrete pair can be read as the paths to stage, or copied into a run that should stage something else, and it ties the shared core to one family of callers.

The generic `<PATHS>` form stays in both commands. Next to it goes a worked example that writes out one concrete multi-path set, for instance the `open_questions.xml` and `requirements.md` pair under `<MILESTONE_DIR>`, as separate literal arguments. The literal-path rule is stated in prose beside them. It keeps the template's link to the PATHS input that every caller uses, and still shows the correct expanded command shape. The generic form and the example of what it expands to each cover the other's weakness. It is the longest wording, with two forms of each command in a 52-line procedure. The `<PATHS>` token that invites single-variable substitution is still the primary form a runner sees.

Both inline command examples are removed. Steps 1 and 2 describe the commands in prose only: a status check scoped to the given paths, and a `git add` with every path of PATHS written out on the command line as its own argument, never through a shell variable. No placeholder form appears in a command at all. No token is left in a command for a runner to copy into a variable, and step 2 already has prose for "naming each path explicitly". The rule and the instruction become the same sentence, with no example that could contradict it. It removes the concrete command shapes the procedure gives elsewhere and that runners rely on, while step 3 keeps its literal `git commit -m` examples, so the file becomes uneven. Runners have to build the status and staging commands themselves, which leaves room for variation that the examples used to prevent.

open-question.question: Where in the CLAUDE.md invariants is the rationale for the literal-command rule recorded: as one new bullet covering both the commit procedure and the tool sites, or as additions to the two existing bullets (the open-question-tool bullet and the committing bullet)?
open-question.alternative: Add one new standalone bullet under `## Invariants to preserve when editing skills`. It covers both provoking sites together: the shell-splitting failure the milestone targets, the shell-neutral rule as it applies to `commit-procedure.md` (each path named literally in the dirty-own-path check and in `git add`, never through a shell variable) and to the multi-call open-question tool sites (the full fixed command on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function), and why the fix is a prose rule rather than a structural one such as a commit tool. The open-question-tool bullet and the committing bullet stay unchanged. The rationale has one home that states the shared cause once. It reads as the single rule it is, a later editor finds the whole decision in one place, and the two already long existing bullets grow no further. An editor reading only the committing bullet or only the open-question-tool bullet, which are the bullets that describe these two sites, sees nothing about literal commands and can "simplify" a site back to a variable without meeting the new bullet. The bullet list also gains one more entry for what is one clause of behaviour at each site. How much the bullet must scope out (the host-provided root variable in the rendered command, the capture snapshot variable, the lift and agent-staging sites) depends on how the sibling questions on those points settle.

Record no new bullet. Extend the open-question-tool bullet, which already fixes "the one fixed command" and "never `python`", with the full-command-on-every-call rule. Extend the committing bullet, which already fixes path-scoped staging and "never `git add -A`", with the literal-path rule for both the guard and the staging. Each addition carries a short statement of the shell-splitting failure, so each bullet stays self-contained. Each rule sits beside the existing invariant it refines, in the bullet an editor of that site already reads. This follows the bullets' established pattern of one invariant growing a "never X" clause rather than a sibling invariant appearing. The shared cause is written twice and can drift between the two bullets. Both bullets are already among the longest in the file, and the open-question-tool bullet also carries the "at most one sentence per site" constraint on runtime prose, which the new tool-site rule must be reconciled with in the same paragraph. Whether that reconciliation is easy depends on where the sibling tool-site placement question puts the rule in the runtime files.

Add one new bullet that holds the whole rationale (the failure, the shell-neutral rule for both sites, and why it is prose rather than a structural fix). Also add a one-clause pointer to it in the open-question-tool bullet (the fixed command is written in full on every call) and in the committing bullet (paths are named literally). The pointers carry no reasons of their own. The rationale is stated once, so nothing drifts, and an editor arriving through either existing bullet still meets the rule and is directed to its reason. Three bullets change for one rule, and the cross-references must be kept in step whenever the new bullet is reworded or the site list changes. It is the heaviest edit of the set for a milestone the goal frames as a narrow prose rule.

Record no new bullet and leave the open-question-tool bullet and the committing bullet unchanged. Instead, extend the existing general bullet on runtime prose ("Runtime files carry no editor-facing prose and name no host") with one shell-neutral authoring rule. Under that rule, a runtime command is written literally, never through a variable, alias, or function the runner introduces. The bullet names the commit procedure's paths and the multi-call tool sites as the provoking cases, and it records the shell-splitting failure and why the fix stays in prose. The rule is filed as what it is, a constraint on how runtime prose writes commands, beside the existing constraints that runtime files name no host and no shell. One home covers both sites and any later command-writing site without the list of bullets growing. An editor reading the committing or open-question-tool bullet for those sites does not meet the rule there. Framed this generally, the rule reads as a ban on every variable in runtime prose, which collides with the capture skill's quoted snapshot variable and with the host-provided root variable in the rendered command unless those are scoped out. Whether this option is viable as worded depends on how the sibling questions on snapshot variable status and host root variable wording settle.

open-question.question: capture-milestone-principle-updates holds a temporary file path in a shell variable (SNAPSHOT="$(mktemp)") and uses it quoted, the one place runtime prose itself instructs a variable. Is the recorded invariant scoped so that this use stays allowed and untouched, or is the rule general enough that the snapshot idiom must be named as an exception or changed?
